articles.text: Thomas Kuhn argued in 1962 that science does not advance by steady accumulation. Most of the time scientists practise normal science, solving puzzles within a shared paradigm. Anomalies pile up, a crisis arrives, and a revolution replaces one paradigm with another that is incommensurable with the first. His examples came from the history of science: the Copernican revolution, the chemical revolution, relativity. The book made paradigm shift a cliche. Critics, including Popper and Lakatos, worried that Kuhn made theory choice a matter of mob psychology. Kuhn replied that scientists share values such as accuracy, scope and simplicity, but weigh them differently. Historians now say the picture is too tidy, with fewer sharp breaks than the model suggests, yet it remains the starting point for anyone thinking about how scientific communities change.

articles.title: The Replication Crisis: What Went Wrong and What Has Improved
articles.gist: Reviews the replication crisis in psychology and biomedicine, covering p-hacking, publication bias and low power, and the reforms of preregistration, registered reports and open data.
articles.text: In 2015 the Open Science Collaboration tried to replicate a hundred psychology studies and found that fewer than half produced a significant result. The causes were not mysterious. Small samples gave low statistical power; researchers had many degrees of freedom to analyse data until something reached p less than 0.05; journals preferred novel positive findings. John Ioannidis had argued in 2005 that most published findings might be false. Reforms followed: preregistration of hypotheses and analysis plans, registered reports that commit a journal to publish before results are known, larger samples, and open data and code. Some fields have improved, others less so. The deeper lesson for philosophers is that scientific method is a social practice, and incentives matter as much as the logic of inference.

articles.title: Bayesians, Frequentists and What a Probability Is
articles.gist: Contrasts Bayesian and frequentist approaches to statistical inference, explaining priors, p-values and credible intervals, and why the debate is really about what probability means.
articles.text: A frequentist treats probability as the long-run frequency of an event in repeated trials, and so a hypothesis is simply true or false; only data have probabilities. A p-value is the chance of data at least as extreme as those seen, assuming the null hypothesis. A Bayesian treats probability as a degree of belief, and uses Bayes' theorem to update a prior distribution in light of evidence, yielding a posterior. The disagreement is partly philosophical and partly practical. Priors seem subjective, yet frequentist procedures hide their own choices, such as stopping rules. Bayesian methods handle small samples and hierarchical models gracefully, and computing posteriors by Markov chain Monte Carlo is now routine. Many working statisticians mix both. The question of which describes scientific reasoning better remains open.

articles.title: Lakatos and the Methodology of Research Programmes
articles.gist: Presents Imre Lakatos's attempt to reconcile Popper and Kuhn, treating science as competing research programmes with a hard core, a protective belt and progressive or degenerating histories.
articles.text: Imre Lakatos thought Popper was too harsh and Kuhn too irrational. His answer was the methodology of scientific research programmes. A programme has a hard core of assumptions that its supporters refuse to abandon, surrounded by a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses that can be modified. A programme is progressive if it predicts novel facts, and degenerating if it only patches itself after the fact. Newtonian mechanics was progressive for centuries, predicting the return of Halley's comet and the existence of Neptune. Lakatos's approach gave historians of science a way to describe real episodes without calling every scientist irrational. Its weakness is that you cannot tell in advance whether a stalled programme is dying or merely waiting. Judgment, not a rule, decides when to abandon it.

articles.title: What Makes a Scientific Model Explanatory?
articles.gist: Surveys philosophical accounts of scientific explanation and the role of idealised models, from covering-law to mechanistic and causal approaches, and asks when a false model can still explain.
articles.text: Every model in science is false in some respect: frictionless planes, perfectly rational agents, infinite populations. Yet they explain. The covering-law account says to explain a phenomenon is to deduce it from laws and initial conditions. Wesley Salmon argued for causal explanation, and philosophers of biology defend mechanistic explanation, in which we identify the parts and their organisation. Idealisations are tools: Nancy Cartwright said the laws of physics lie, in the sense that they describe idealised situations, and models are what connect them to the world. A good model isolates the factors that make a difference. The test is not whether it is realistic but whether it supports counterfactual reasoning, showing what would happen if we intervened. Underdetermination remains, since many models fit the same data.

articles.title: Is Economics a Science?
articles.gist: Examines whether economics meets the standards of a science, weighing its predictive record, reliance on idealised models, the credibility revolution in empirical work, and the problem of reflexive theories.
articles.text: Economists predict recessions poorly, and critics conclude that economics is not a science. Defenders reply that prediction is not the only test, and that economics has done well at explaining and at causal inference. The credibility revolution, led by Angrist, Card and Imbens, brought natural experiments and randomised trials to labour economics, and their work on the minimum wage and schooling relied on clear identification strategies. Yet theory still leans on idealised models with rational agents, and these are hard to falsify. There is also reflexivity: when people learn a theory, such as the efficient markets hypothesis, they change their behaviour. Milton Friedman argued that the realism of assumptions is irrelevant if predictions hold; philosophers have not found that persuasive. Economics is a science of a particular, difficult kind.

articles.title: Marr's Three Levels and Why Neuroscience Keeps Forgetting Them
articles.gist: Revisits David Marr's distinction between computational, algorithmic and implementational levels of explanation, and argues that neuroscience and machine learning both suffer when they mix them up.
articles.text: David Marr argued in Vision that understanding an information-processing system requires three levels. The computational level asks what the system is for and why that is the right goal. The algorithmic level asks what representations and procedures it uses. The implementational level asks how those are physically realised, in neurons or in silicon. His point was that you cannot understand a bird by studying feathers alone. Neuroscience, fascinated by recording from cells, often skips the first two levels, while machine learning researchers sometimes forget the third. A framework like Bayesian inference is a computational-level theory; predictive coding is an algorithmic proposal; cortical layers would be the implementation. Keeping the levels distinct clarifies what a given experiment can show and which kinds of disagreement are substantive.

articles.title: How Central Banks Fight Inflation, and Why It Is Harder Than It Looks
articles.gist: Explains how central banks use interest rates and balance sheets to manage inflation, drawing on the post-pandemic experience and the role of expectations, lags and supply shocks.
articles.text: A central bank controls inflation chiefly by setting short-term interest rates. Raising them makes borrowing dearer, cools demand, and in time pulls prices down. The difficulty is lags: policy takes a year or more to bite, so the bank must act on forecasts. After the pandemic, inflation climbed above nine percent in the United States, and the Federal Reserve raised rates from near zero to over five percent in eighteen months. Economists argued about whether the cause was monetary policy, fiscal stimulus or supply shocks. Expectations matter enormously: if households and firms believe the bank will hold prices steady, they behave in ways that make it so, which is why credibility is a central bank's main asset. Quantitative easing, forward guidance and the Taylor rule remain the major tools of the trade.

articles.title: Comparative Advantage: The Idea Economists Refuse to Give Up
articles.gist: Explains David Ricardo's principle of comparative advantage, why trade can benefit both countries even when one is better at everything, and what the idea leaves out about distribution.
articles.text: Suppose Portugal can make both wine and cloth more cheaply than England. Ricardo showed in 1817 that both still gain from trade if each specialises in the good for which its opportunity cost is lowest. This is comparative advantage, and economists find it counterintuitive and correct. The principle explains why a surgeon who types faster than her secretary should still hire one. It does not say everyone gains: when trade expands, particular workers in particular industries lose, as the China shock research of David Autor shows. Trade economists today emphasise adjustment costs, regional concentration of harm and the case for compensation. The theory is not an argument for ignoring losers; it shows that the total gains are large enough that, in principle, the winners could pay for the losers.

articles.title: Why Housing Costs So Much: Supply, Zoning and the Rent
articles.gist: Argues from the economics of land-use regulation that restrictive zoning limits housing supply in productive cities, raising prices and rents, and reviews what reforms have achieved.
articles.text: Housing in coastal American cities is expensive not because construction is uniquely costly but because supply is restricted. Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko show that in places like San Francisco the price of a home far exceeds the cost of building it, and the gap is the regulatory tax of zoning, height limits and lengthy approval. Landowners and incumbents benefit, so local politics rarely changes it. The effects reach beyond housing: workers cannot move to high-productivity cities, which holds down national growth. Houston, with minimal zoning, has stayed cheaper while growing. Reforms such as Minneapolis's elimination of single-family zoning and Auckland's upzoning have been followed by slower rent growth. Economists generally agree that more supply helps, and the debate concerns how to build it fairly.

articles.title: Network Effects and the Economics of Platforms
articles.gist: Explains direct and indirect network effects, two-sided markets and multi-homing, and why platform businesses tend toward concentration and how startups can still break in.
articles.text: A telephone is worthless if nobody else has one, and more valuable with each new subscriber. This is a direct network effect. Platforms such as payment networks, marketplaces and app stores add indirect effects: more buyers attract more sellers, who attract more buyers. Jean Tirole's work on two-sided markets shows that platforms often subsidise one side, charging the other, to get the flywheel turning. Network effects push toward winner-take-most outcomes, but they are weaker than they seem when users can multi-home, using several services at once, and when the effects are local rather than global. For founders, the lesson is to find a small, dense network where value is felt quickly, such as one university for Facebook, and expand from it. Incumbents' scale is hardest to beat head-on.

articles.title: Auction Design and the Nobel Prize in Game Theory
articles.gist: Introduces auction theory and mechanism design, from second-price auctions to the spectrum auctions designed by Paul Milgrom and Robert Wilson, showing how game theory shaped real markets.
articles.text: In a second-price sealed-bid auction, the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid. William Vickrey showed that in such an auction the best strategy is to bid your true value, which makes it a rare case where honesty is optimal. Game theory analyses this kind of strategic interaction, asking what each player will do given what the others do, a Nash equilibrium. Paul Milgrom and Robert Wilson applied the ideas to the sale of radio spectrum, designing simultaneous ascending auctions that raised tens of billions for governments and put licences with the firms that valued them most. Search engines run auctions for advertising every few milliseconds. The tradition of mechanism design, which asks how to build rules so that selfish participants produce good outcomes, is among economics's best examples of theory used in practice.

articles.title: Behavioural Economics After the Nudge
articles.gist: Reviews behavioural economics, from Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory to nudges, and weighs the reproducibility problems that have dented some famous findings against the durable core.
articles.text: Standard economics assumes rational agents with stable preferences. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky documented systematic departures: loss aversion, anchoring, framing, and overweighting of small probabilities. Prospect theory formalised the first, and Richard Thaler showed that these biases explain anomalies in savings, markets and tipping. The nudge movement, popularised by Thaler and Cass Sunstein, argued that default options can steer people toward better choices without removing freedom: automatic enrolment in pensions raises participation dramatically. Subsequent replication efforts have been less kind to some well-known effects, such as ego depletion and certain priming studies, and meta-analyses suggest nudges are smaller than first reported. What survives is an emphasis on defaults, friction and attention. Policy makers now use behavioural insights teams, though with more humility about effect sizes.

articles.title: The Royal Society and the Birth of Experimental Philosophy
articles.gist: Tells how the Royal Society, founded in 1660, promoted public experiment and plain reporting, with Robert Boyle's air-pump trials as the model for how modern science establishes matters of fact.
articles.text: The Royal Society of London, founded in 1660, took as its motto nullius in verba, take nobody's word for it. Its fellows, Robert Boyle, Robert Hooke and later Isaac Newton, believed knowledge came from experiment performed in front of witnesses. Boyle's air pump was the great instrument: before gentlemen of the Society, he showed that a bird in a bell jar died as the air was drawn out. In Leviathan and the Air-Pump, Steven Shapin and Simon Schaffer describe how Boyle persuaded readers with detailed reports and virtual witnessing, while Thomas Hobbes objected that experiment could not settle philosophical questions. The disagreement shaped modern science, which accepts public replicable demonstration as its standard. Historians treat the early Royal Society as the place where the habits of modern science, such as citing and replication, took form.

articles.title: Darwin, Wallace and the Problem of Simultaneous Discovery
articles.gist: Recounts how Alfred Russel Wallace independently reached natural selection in 1858, prompting Darwin to publish, and uses it to ask how often scientific discoveries are made in parallel.
articles.text: In June 1858, in Down House in Kent, Charles Darwin opened a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace, then in the Malay Archipelago, and saw his own theory of natural selection described in a few pages. Darwin had been working on it for twenty years. Friends arranged a joint presentation at the Linnean Society, and On the Origin of Species followed in 1859. The case is a prime example of multiple discovery: calculus came from Newton and Leibniz, oxygen from Priestley and Scheele. Robert Merton argued that such cases are the rule, not the exception, because the necessary ideas are in the air. Historians dispute how generous Darwin was to Wallace. Both were reading Malthus on population, which suggests that the discovery owed as much to context as to genius.

articles.title: Lavoisier, Oxygen and the Chemical Revolution
articles.gist: Describes how Antoine Lavoisier overthrew phlogiston theory by weighing reactants carefully, naming oxygen and reforming chemical nomenclature, and how a tax collector's rigour changed chemistry.
articles.text: For most of the eighteenth century, chemists explained burning by phlogiston, a substance supposedly released from combustible bodies. Antoine Lavoisier, a tax farmer with a laboratory, did something stubbornly quantitative: he weighed everything. He showed that metals gain weight when they burn, because they combine with a component of air, which he named oxygen. Priestley and Scheele had isolated the gas, but they interpreted it through phlogiston; Lavoisier reorganised the whole framework. With colleagues he published a new system of nomenclature, so that substances were named for their elements. His wife Marie-Anne Paulze illustrated his work and translated English papers. Lavoisier was guillotined in 1794. Kuhn used the chemical revolution as a central example of a paradigm shift, though historians note it unfolded over decades.

articles.title: Bell Labs: How an Institution Invented the Information Age
articles.gist: A history of Bell Labs, the research lab that produced the transistor, information theory and the Unix operating system, and what its structure and management can teach founders and research leaders today.
articles.text: Between the 1920s and the 1980s Bell Labs produced the transistor, the laser, information theory, the cellular telephone concept and Unix. Its scientists included Claude Shannon, William Shockley and Dennis Ritchie. Jon Gertner, in The Idea Factory, describes a place that mixed physicists, chemists and engineers in one building, funded by AT&T's monopoly profits. Mervin Kelly, the director, believed in proximity: corridors were long so that people would run into one another. Researchers were given freedom to pursue long-term problems but were also close to the telephone business that needed their results. The monopoly ended, and the lab shrank. Founders and research managers still study it, because few organisations have combined deep science with practical engineering so well.

articles.title: Euclid's Elements: Twenty-Three Centuries as a Textbook
articles.gist: Looks at how Euclid's Elements was used as the model textbook of reasoning for over two thousand years, and what its method of axioms and proofs teaches about the history of mathematical education.
articles.text: Few books have been used as long as a textbook as Euclid's Elements. Written in Alexandria around 300 BCE, it presents geometry from five postulates and a handful of definitions, proving each proposition from earlier ones. Medieval students copied it; Abraham Lincoln studied it to learn how to argue; schoolchildren in England met it into the twentieth century. It taught a method of reasoning at least as much as geometry. Historians of mathematics note that the book has gaps by modern standards, and the parallel postulate inspired non-Euclidean geometry in the nineteenth century. Educators still debate whether to teach proof as a ritual or as discovery. The Elements survives because it shows how a chain of simple steps can lead somewhere surprising.

articles.title: Spaced Repetition and the Forgetting Curve
articles.gist: Explains Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve and the spacing effect, how spaced repetition software schedules reviews, and what evidence says about its effectiveness for long-term learning.
articles.text: In the 1880s Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised lists of nonsense syllables and measured how fast he forgot them. Memory decays exponentially, quickly at first and then slowly, and each review flattens the curve. The spacing effect, one of the most robust findings in psychology, says that spreading study over time beats massing it into one session. Spaced repetition software such as Anki and SuperMemo exploit this: each card is shown just before you would forget it, and the interval grows after every successful recall. Studies of medical students find sizeable gains in retention from spaced flashcards. The costs are discipline and the effort of making good cards: ask one clear question per card, prefer understanding to rote. Many learners find that a few minutes a day beats long cramming sessions.

articles.title: Desirable Difficulties: Why Struggling Helps You Learn
articles.gist: Reviews Robert Bjork's concept of desirable difficulties, including spacing, interleaving and testing, and explains why conditions that feel harder in the moment improve durable learning.
articles.text: Students prefer methods that feel fluent: rereading, highlighting, practising one kind of problem in a block. Robert Bjork's research shows that these feelings are misleading. Conditions that slow initial performance, which he calls desirable difficulties, tend to improve long-term retention and transfer. Interleaving different problem types forces learners to choose a strategy, not just apply one. Spacing practice makes retrieval harder but more durable. Testing yourself beats restudying. The trouble is that learners judge by how smoothly it went, and so they choose the less effective method. Teachers face a related problem, since students rate fluent lectures higher. The lesson is to distinguish performance from learning and to build some struggle into every lesson, as long as it is the kind a learner can eventually overcome.

articles.title: Retrieval Practice: The Testing Effect and the Brain
articles.gist: Explains the testing effect, in which retrieving information strengthens memory more than rereading, and links behavioural results to neuroscience on reconsolidation and hippocampal-cortical interaction.
articles.text: In a classic experiment by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, students studied a passage and then either reread it or tried to recall it. A week later, those who had been tested remembered far more, even though they felt less confident. This is the testing effect. Each act of retrieval is not just a readout but a modification: when a memory is brought to mind it becomes briefly labile and is reconsolidated, often more strongly. Imaging work shows that successful retrieval engages the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex and, over time, shifts reliance toward cortical representations. Practical applications include closing the book to write what you remember, using flashcards, and low-stakes quizzes in the classroom. The effort feels uncomfortable, and that is the sign it is working.

articles.title: Deliberate Practice and the Limits of the Ten-Thousand-Hour Rule
articles.gist: Examines Anders Ericsson's research on deliberate practice, its misrepresentation as a ten-thousand-hour rule, and what it implies about how adults can improve at skills through structured feedback.
articles.text: Anders Ericsson studied violinists at a Berlin music academy and found that the best had accumulated more hours of solitary, effortful practice than the rest. Malcolm Gladwell popularised the figure of ten thousand hours, which Ericsson disowned: it was an average, not a threshold, and it was deliberate practice that counted, not mere repetition. Deliberate practice has a specific shape: a well-defined goal, full attention, immediate feedback, and work at the edge of one's ability, usually guided by a teacher. Later meta-analyses found that practice explains a smaller share of variance than Ericsson claimed, especially in fields with less structure. Still, for most skills a principle holds: more of the right kind of practice, with feedback, improves performance. Adults can borrow the format for writing, coding and languages.

articles.title: Lessons from Finding Product-Market Fit the Hard Way
articles.gist: A founder's retrospective on three years before finding product-market fit, with lessons on talking to customers, measuring retention, and knowing when to pivot instead of persist.
articles.text: For three years we built features nobody asked for. Marc Andreessen describes product-market fit as being in a good market with a product that satisfies it, and says you can feel it when it happens: customers pull the product out of your hands. We did not feel that. Our lessons came late. First, retention is the truth: a cohort chart that flattens means people stay, and one that falls to zero means they do not, whatever your signups say. Second, talk to customers every week, and ask about problems, not features. Third, pivot earlier than feels comfortable: we waited eighteen months too long. Paul Graham's advice to make something people want sounds trite until you realise how rarely it is followed. Managing a small team through the search also taught me that morale follows evidence of progress.
